title: Burst recovery and quantization fingerprinting — field logbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working logbook for a small experimental suite we ran to characterize how low-precision kernels (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 variants) behave under short, high-concurrency bursts and how those behaviors leave reproducible "fingerprints" on latency, throughput and output-quality. Goal is to collect concrete mitigation knobs and an operational fingerprint catalogue we can feed into the smart routing and fallback heuristics in the runtime.

Motivation / background:
- We've seen recurring customer incidents where short bursts (10–60s) produce tail-latency spikes or transient quality regressions that then clear up after a minute. Root cause is unclear in many cases: kernel scheduling congestion, memory-bank conflict, KV-cache warmup, or quantization numerical instability.
- Most previous experiments focused on steady-state throughput vs quality. This set targets burst dynamics: ramps, recovery time, and the unique metric signatures different quant schemes produce.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Single-shot/concurrent bursts expose kernel-level serialization and cold-tile/packing inefficiencies more for AWQ and some INT8 kernels than for FP8; thus higher transient latency but lower steady-state cost.
2) GPTQ representations tend to keep better output fidelity during bursts but sometimes incur heavier memory traffic (larger per-layer activations), causing micro-congestion and longer recovery.
3) Fingerprints (time-series of per-token latency, queue length, small-sample logprob delta) are distinguishable enough to drive a lightweight runtime classifier that recommends an immediate fallback (e.g., switch to FP8 variant or different kernel) when we see certain patterns.

Experiment design:
- Synthetic workloads: three types (chatty short-turns, long-context single-stream, and many-short-concurrent). Each workload has a controlled burst: ramp from baseline qps to peak qps in 2s, sustain 30s, then decay.
- Models: Llama-variant 13B and an instruction-tuned 7B for diversity.
- Quantization variants:
  * INT8 (static per-layer symmetric)
  * AWQ (2-4 bit per-group plus reconstruction heuristics)
  * GPTQ (8-bit optimized offline per model)
  * FP8 (bfloat-inspired config we use for fallback)
- Kernels: two kernel families on the same GPU arch (vector-lane-parallel vs packed-tile). We force kernel choice in the runtime for tests.
- Metrics collected (per-request, per-token, aggregated): p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth, GPU SM utilization, L1/L2 bandwidth counters, per-layer activation bytes, model logprobs on a short canned eval set, and a lightweight per-request perplexity delta relative to FP32 baseline.

Key findings (short):
- Latency spikes consistently correlated with two distinct signatures: "stair-step" microjams (vector-lane kernel) and "sawtooth" congestion (packed-tile kernel). Stair-step had sub-100ms jitter but accumulated to 200–400ms p99 increases; sawtooth produced larger instantaneous 400–800ms spikes.
- AWQ and INT8 kernels showed faster steady-state throughput (20–35% higher than FP8/GPTQ in our bench) but their p99 during the 30s sustained burst was 1.8–2.6x baseline p99. GPTQ had lower p99 inflation (1.2–1.6x) but used ~10–18% more memory bandwidth, leading to slightly longer recovery time post-burst (average extra 12–18s).
- Recovery time (time to return to <1.1x baseline p95) varies: INT8/AWQ vector-lane kernels recover in ~6–12s; packed-tile INT8 variants sometimes take 20–40s due to cache-eviction thrashing. FP8 fallbacks typically recover fastest but at a cost (50–70% higher per-token execution time).
- Quality: small synthetic eval set (200 prompts) shows AWQ had median logprob delta ~0.08 nat/token vs FP32, GPTQ ~0.05, INT8 ~0.12; during bursts quality deltas widen by ~10–25% for AWQ/INT8 but remain stable for GPTQ/FP8.

Fingerprint catalogue (operational):
- Stair-step fingerprint: repeating micro-latency increments (~10–30ms) at kernel-bound bursts, correlated with SM occupancy oscillations. Most common on vector-lane-int8. Runtime reaction: increase batching window by 5ms and enable light-weight kernel pacing.
- Sawtooth fingerprint: large intermittent spikes with long tails and elevated L2 traffic — indicates packed-tile kernel thrash. Reaction: graceful switchover to alternative packed-kernel or immediate fallback to FP8 variant for the next 100 requests.
- Memory-bank hotspot fingerprint: p99 latency + rising memory write stalls + KV-cache miss ratio spike. Reaction: prefer GPTQ (if available) or throttle concurrency for 8–12s while seeding prefix cache; log incident for future model re-quantization.
- Quality-drift fingerprint: small but consistent rise in perplexity / logprob delta during burst. If above threshold (configurable per-customer) trigger quality-protection: route to higher-fidelity model or add a quick post-filtering reranker.

Mitigations tested and results:
1) Rapid kernel switchover: on detection of sawtooth fingerprint, switchover to FP8 kernel within 120ms; p99 reduced by median 320ms in subsequent 10s but CPU overhead increased. Tradeoff: avoids long tail but increases cost.
2) Short-term concurrency throttles: capping concurrent requests per GPU reduced p99 spike magnitude by ~40% with minimal throughput loss for burst durations <45s. Good low-cost mitigation.
3) Prefix seeding: for long-context bursts, prepopulating KV-cache for top-10 prompts reduced recovery time by ~25% and lowered quality drift. Operationally useful for repetitive chatty workloads.
4) Adaptive batching window: increasing micro-batching during burst onset reduced the number of kernel invocations and smoothed stair-step behavior. Improved p95 by ~15% with slight p50 increase.

Practical recommendations (for product/runtime):
- Implement lightweight fingerprint detector (rule-based, then simple classifier) on the request-router that consumes per-token latency + small set of perf counters. Keep classifier memory-free (no heavy models).
- Default escalation path: for detected sawtooth -> immediate kernel switchover or FP8 fallback for a fixed short window (30s), then backoff. For stair-step -> enable micro-batching + slight concurrency throttle.
- Expose per-customer sensitivity toggles: aggressive-quality-protection (favor GPTQ/FP8 fallback), cost-saver (favor INT8/AWQ but allow transient tails).
- Add a daily offline job to recompute per-model fingerprint baselines using production-like synthetic bursts in our CI harness.

Open questions and next experiments:
- Can we design a kernel packing layout that avoids the packed-tile sawtooth entirely on newer GPU generations? Need architecture partner input.
- Is there a cheap runtime estimator that predicts when AWQ numeric instabilities will manifest for a given prompt distribution? Consider small per-layer diagnostic probes inserted during warmup.
- Evaluate ripple effects across multi-tenant packing: how does a noisy kernel from one tenant influence co-located tenants? Early traces show cross-tenant p99 coupling on some configs.

Quick log entries (raw):
- 2025-07-15 10:14 — ran chatty-short-turn burst on 13B AWQ vector-lane; observed stair-step p99 drift from 180ms -> 420ms over 28s.
- 2025-07-16 14:03 — forced packed-tile INT8 on 7B; saw intermittent 740ms spikes correlated with L2 traffic surges.
- 2025-07-18 09:22 — applied micro-batching + 5ms window during ramp; saw p95 improve 18% across runs.
- 2025-07-20 16:05 — validated kernel switchover to FP8: cost up 1.6x, but p99 back within target for 90% of the 30s windows.

Appendix (commands / snippets):
- Synthetic client: ./bench/burst_client --model 13b --quant awq --kernel vector-lane --ramp 2 --sustain 30 --qps 250
- Perf capture: ./scripts/capture_counters --gpu 0 --events SM__STALLED_CYCLES, L2__READS, L2__WRITES --out /tmp/run-20250715.csv
- Quick quality probe: python eval/mini_eval.py --prompts samples/200-short.json --model 13b --quant awq --baseline-fp32 /mnt/baselines/13b-fp32.logprobs

Notes to follow-up owners:
- Marco: try kernel-packing variant 3 (PR 1192) on the same bench; compare L2 counters.
- Sana: sketch the lightweight fingerprint detector (rule sets + small feature vector), include thresholds, and run on a week's production traces (anonymized).
- Priya (self): consolidate the fingerprint catalogue into a YAML that runtime can consume and propose default thresholds for cost/quality tiers.

Bottom line:
Burst behavior matters — low-precision wins in steady-state costs but can create reproducible operational failures during short high-intensity bursts. We can detect and mitigate these with a mix of kernel switchover, micro-batching, and short throttles; cataloguing fingerprints enables automated, low-latency reactions that avoid manual incident handling.

End of logbook entry.
